newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria hits gangsters Chicago-style -- over tax.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria hits gangsters Chicago-style -- over tax.

text.p: The new team at Bulgaria's Interior Ministry is taking its cue from 1930s Chicago and using tougher tax law enforcement to crack down on organised crime.
"It wasn't murder or robbery they got Al Capone for, it was unpaid taxes," Interior Minister Bogomil Bonev said in an interview on Tuesday.
The interim government which took office in February has vowed to stamp out the crime and corruption which have flourished in the seven years since the end of one-party rule.
"It is an open secret that the Bulgarian legal system has only a limited ability to fight organised crime," Bonev said.
He said the ministry was hampered by out of date legislation, but was working on drafting new laws to be put before parliament after the April 19 elections.
Last month, Bonev's ministry organised a high-profile check on luxury cars dubbed Operation Mosquito, to crack down on car theft and tax evasion.

The ministry said some 14,600 cars were inspected around the country, and 100 were found to have altered serial numbers, suggesting they had been stolen. The second stage of the operation will check luxury villas.
Asked about charges that the operation was a publicity stunt, Bonev said that its high profile had a psychological effect on small-time criminals who realised they were no longer untouchable.
"Up to now, the fight against the so-called 'strong arm' groups has existed only on paper," he said.

He said as well as cracking down on ill-gotten gains, the ministry also had to win back the commitment of the demoralised police force. "Low pay and the feeling that many criminals were invincible was bad for morale," he said.

He said the lifting of export controls as Bulgaria began adapting to a market economy after 1989 had played into the hands of the former heads of the 250 state foreign trade companies, who were familiar with the market environment and well placed to profit from it.
Bonev said retrieving the money siphoned out of Bulgaria was no easy task because of banking secrecy laws and differences in legislation with other countries.
"It's not realistic to think we can bring back 100 percent, we would be happy to achieve even a part of the total," he said.
He said the ministry planned a new tax system after the elections, which he hoped would encourage people to repatriate their money and invest it in Bulgaria.
Economic Policy Minister Krassimir Angarski has proposed a one-off 25 percent tax to legalise previously undeclared property holdings, and Bonev said this idea could be expanded to repatriated funds.
"It's a good business opportunity," Bonev said. "It's well known that an economy in transition creates opportunities for high yields."

Investors are already eyeing Bulgarian treasury paper, which will offer high interest at a fixed exchange rate once a currency board system is introduced in June, pegging the lev to the dollar or the mark.
Bonev said that the ministry had also started to crack down on smuggling, and on video and compact disc piracy.

He said the ministry was making progress in investigating the October 1996 death of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov, shot outside his home in an apparent contract killing, but declined to give details.
